parts.title: Reporting lost property
parts.context: A woman phones a railway lost property office about a bag she left on a train.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a railway lost property office about a bag she left on a train. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Lost property office, Ian speaking.

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: Oh, hello. I left something on a train yesterday evening, and I'm hoping somebody has handed it in. It's a backpack.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: OK, a backpack. Let's fill in a report and I'll check what's come in.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman lost a backpack, so 'backpack' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: First of all, can I have your name?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: Sofia Moreno.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: Yes. M-O-R-E-N-O.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Thank you. And which train were you on?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: I got on at Cambridge at about six. It was the train going to Norwich, and I got off at Ely.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: So the train continued to Norwich. Do you remember where you were sitting?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: I had a reserved seat. It was seat twenty-four. No, sorry, twenty-four was my ticket on the way out. On the way back it was forty-two, near the toilets.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Seat forty-two. And can you describe the backpack?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: It's quite big, the kind people take hiking. People always think it's grey because the straps and the zips are grey, but the bag itself is green. Quite a dark green.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Any brand name, or anything that would help us recognise it?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: There isn't a brand name on it, but my sister sewed a little picture of a fox on the front pocket. It's orange, so it really stands out.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: That's helpful. What was inside the bag?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: My laptop was in my hand, luckily. But my camera was in it, in a black case. And a library book.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: A camera in a black case, and a library book. Anything else?

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: My keys. They're on a ring with a small torch, the sort you use to find a keyhole in the dark.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: Right. Now, if the bag is found, how would you like us to contact you? We can phone, send an email or a text.

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: Not email, I hardly check it. A text would be best, because I can't always answer the phone at work.

script.speaker: ian
script.text: No problem. I should tell you that we keep items for thirty days. After that, anything valuable goes to auction and the money goes to charity.

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: Thirty days. OK. And is there anything to pay when I collect it?

script.speaker: ian
script.text: There's a small handling fee. It used to be ten pounds, but it's been reduced, and now it's five pounds for any item.

script.speaker: sofia
script.text: That's fine. Thank you so much for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A food festival
parts.context: A radio presenter talks about a town's food festival.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a presenter on local radio talking about a food festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And now, something for everyone who likes eating. The Millbrook Food Festival is back this weekend, for the twelfth year, and I've been talking to the organisers to find out what's new.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: The festival used to be held in the market square, but it had simply outgrown it. This year, for the first time, it's moving to Riverside Park. That gives the organisers three times as much space, and it means there's finally room for a proper seating area, which was the most common request on last year's feedback forms.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Entry is still free, as it has always been, but the organisers are asking people not to drive. There are only a few parking spaces near the park, so a free shuttle bus will run from the railway station every fifteen minutes. If you do come by car, the leisure centre car park is your best bet, but it fills up early.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: This year's theme is food without waste. Every stall has agreed to use plates and cutlery that can be composted, and there will be no plastic bottles on sale at all. Instead, you can fill your own bottle for free at water points around the park. So do bring one with you.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And for the first time, the festival will have a children's area, run by the cookery school on Bridge Street. Children can make their own pizzas, but places are limited, and you'll need to book them on the festival website, not on the day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Now, the festival runs from Friday evening right through to Sunday, so let me tell you when the main events are on.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: If you're a fan of cheese, the cheese tasting tent opens at six on Friday, and it's on that evening only, because the cheesemakers are off to another show on Saturday morning.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: The chilli eating contest has been moved. It was originally planned for Saturday, but the organisers decided it would draw a bigger crowd on the last day, so it will now take place on Sunday at two.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: The cookery demonstrations by local chefs run every afternoon, but the one everyone wants to see is Marco Bellini, who used to cook at the Ritz. He's appearing on Saturday at three. Arrive early if you want a seat.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: There's a bread-making workshop for adults, which is run twice, on Friday evening and again on Saturday morning. It's the same workshop both times, so pick whichever suits you.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: On Sunday morning, there's a farmers' breakfast, with eggs, bacon and bread all from farms within ten miles of the town.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And the festival ends, as always, with the dessert competition, where you get to vote for your favourite. That's on Sunday evening, just before the fireworks. Right, after the news, it's time for the weather.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A survey on sleep
parts.context: Two psychology students discuss their survey on students' sleep with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Leo and Hana, discussing a survey on students' sleep with their tutor, Professor Grant. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: So, Leo, Hana, tell me how the sleep survey went.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Really well, actually. We got two hundred and twelve responses, which is more than we'd hoped for.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: How did you manage that?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Posters didn't do much, and emails just got ignored. What worked was asking lecturers to give us five minutes at the end of large lectures, so students could fill it in on their phones there and then. And we offered a prize draw, which probably helped too.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: And the main findings?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Two things surprised us. We thought students who worked part-time jobs would sleep less, but there was no real difference. What did matter was screen use. Students who used their phones in bed slept almost an hour less than the others. And the second surprise was that first-year students slept less than final-year students, not more.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: We'd assumed final-year students would be the most stressed. But a lot of first-years said they stayed up late socialising.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Interesting. Were there any problems with the questionnaire?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: One, really. We asked people how many hours they slept 'on a typical night', but people's weekdays and weekends are so different that the answers were hard to interpret. Next time we'd ask about weekdays and weekends separately.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: That's a good point to put in your evaluation. And what are you going to do with the results?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: We'd like to share them with the student support team. They're planning a wellbeing campaign next term, and they've asked to see our data.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Now, for the second stage, you're planning a sleep diary study. Talk me through the steps.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: First we need to recruit volunteers. We'll invite people who did the survey and said they'd be willing to take part, so we'll start by emailing them.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Then everyone who agrees will come to a short training session, where we show them how to fill in the diary. In the pilot, people recorded things differently, so we need everyone to do it the same way.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: After that, they'll keep the diary for two weeks. Every morning they write down when they went to bed, when they woke up, and how rested they feel.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: At the end of the two weeks, they'll fill in a short questionnaire about their mood and concentration, so we can compare that with their sleep.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: And then we'll interview a small number of them, perhaps six, to find out more about what affected their sleep.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: And how will you use the interviews?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: We'll use them to write a set of practical tips for students, which we'll give to the support team for their campaign.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: That sounds like a well-planned study. Make sure you get ethics approval before you contact anyone.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: urban heat islands
parts.context: A lecture on why cities are warmer than the countryside, and what can be done.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today's topic is the urban heat island: the fact that cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. The difference is usually greatest at night, and on a calm summer night a large city can be as much as ten degrees warmer than nearby villages.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why does this happen? The first reason is the materials cities are built from. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat from the sun during the day and then release it slowly after dark, so the city never really cools down. Dark roofs and roads are the worst, because they reflect so little sunlight.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The second reason is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants release water into the air, and this evaporation has a cooling effect, rather like sweating does for us. In a city centre, where most surfaces are paved, there's very little of this natural cooling.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Third, cities produce heat of their own. Cars, factories and, increasingly, air conditioners all release waste heat. In fact, air conditioning creates a vicious circle: it cools the inside of buildings by pumping heat outside, which makes the streets hotter, so people use even more air conditioning.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, the shape of the city matters. Tall buildings along narrow streets trap heat and block the wind that would otherwise carry it away. These are sometimes called urban canyons.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why does this matter? Above all, for health. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply in cities, and the people most at risk are the elderly, especially those living alone. The heat also increases energy use, and it makes air pollution worse, because ozone forms more quickly in hot weather.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: What can be done? One of the cheapest solutions is simply to paint roofs white, so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Studies in some cities have shown that this can reduce the temperature inside top-floor flats by several degrees.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Trees are also very effective. They provide shade, and they cool the air through evaporation. Some cities now plan their tree planting using heat maps, so that the trees go where people suffer most, rather than in the wealthier areas that already have parks.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Green roofs, covered in plants, are another option, although they are expensive to install and need regular maintenance. And finally, water can help. Paris, for example, has opened up rivers that had been covered over, and fountains and pools give people places to cool down.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Next week we'll look at how one city, Medellín in Colombia, reduced street temperatures by creating green corridors.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
